[SPEAKER_00]
I like how Alex was like, we're gonna show you all the good things that are happening this year and then I'm talking about the state of fintech funding. It's not a really, not exactly a rosy topic. So I was thinking about, you know, it's it's the keynote, it's the state of, so I was thinking about the state of the union and the president always starts out by saying the state of the union is strong and so I thought I'd start out by saying the state of fintech funding is weird. It's really weird right now. The last few years have been pretty crazy. I'm thinking back to March 2020, two and a half years ago, time before COVID, time before a lot of stuff. We were raising fund one for BTV, just getting it off the ground. We thought we'd do a close on March 30th, 2020. Turned out that pretty much everyone pulled their capital out of our fund and we were like, I guess we're just gonna have like a Sheil and Jake family office fund, which, you know, would be much, much smaller than we were planning for. And we actually send a letter out to our LPs that had committed in April and we said we're gonna buckle up and valuations are gonna come down really significantly. There's gonna be a lot less capital available to folks and so it's a great time to start a fund. We were completely fucking wrong, right? Like what happened next? Stimulus, the Fed printing money, the money printing machine going burr, as we all know. And we ended up a few months later increasing the size of our fund and ended up being oversubscribed, which we didn't expect. And what happened was all eyes were on fintech. We were like suddenly from, you know, I've been in fintech for about a dozen years. No one gave a shit about us for a very long time. And then all of a sudden, the last few years, we were the bell of the ball. Like we were, everybody was investing in fintech. Everybody was changing their Twitter profile to say fintech investor. And that was really cool. That was really fun. We had a lot of newcomers in early stage venture investing. We had a bunch of new funds. It felt like anyone who had done anything in fintech could raise a fund easily. When I started my first fund in 2017, it took me 18 months. I had to beg people. And it's felt like in 2020 or 2021, literally anyone was able to raise a $20 million fund. And on the other side of the coin, we had all the PJ guys, if you know what I mean, the private jet guys, the guys who run hedge funds, they felt like they were missing out on private investments. It was like a great opportunity for them. This is where all the action was. So your company, KOTU, D1s, and then like a hundred other firms that don't have websites, all decided to invest in fintech too. And after being public markets investors, they felt like there was an opportunity in privates. There was just like a ton of capital flowing in. So it led to a crazy year of funding. There was $142 billion funded in fintech companies alone in 2021. And the previous year, it was $49 billion. And if you go back just a few years earlier, it was about a third of that. Last year, we had 160 new unicorns, again, up from 28 in 2020. Totally a nuts year. We had fintech SPACs. We had companies going public. It literally felt like everything we invested in was gold. And like you could find an exit, somebody would invest at a higher price. We, in our own portfolio, all the companies that we'd seeded that went out to raise a series A in the second half of 2021, raised at greater than $100 million valuation. And some of these are pre -revenue businesses. It's completely insane now that I'm thinking about it at this moment. So those low interest rates and the money printer were really, really good for our business. Or so it seemed. The outcome of those things was, as unfortunately we now know, a tough inflationary environment. And the Fed having to hike rates five times this year. They've hiked it more than they have in the past 30 years. So it's been a particularly rough environment. And today, fintech companies are down 72%. Public fintech companies are down on the year about 72%. And last year, high growing fintech companies were at a crazy, this is on the public market side, were at a crazy 25x revenue multiple. And today that multiple is down to about 4.5x. So things have changed very drastically, very quickly. So there are about 59 public fintech companies out there. And how many of them do you guys think are in the green this year? Anyone? 11? It's actually one. And until last week, that company was in the red. Companies build trust. They're getting acquired by EQT. But otherwise, the other 58 companies are all in the red by an average of 72%. It's been a rough year. So what does all that have to do with early stage fintech? Well, as the public market started falling at the beginning of this year, so did late stage valuations. We saw it in our portfolio in like kind of January, February, we had a company going out for a series D, they had doubled revenue, we thought it'd be a slam dunk. And instead, they fell flat on their face. And we ended up doing an inside round at the same price as the previous round, even though they had more than doubled revenue. And at first, I thought, that's rough. In hindsight, that flat round was like amazing. And I should have congratulated the founder. So a lot of companies raise money at a great time. Like it was easy, easy time to raise money last year. And so because of that, the growth stage companies that are raising this year haven't been looked at so favorably. And so that's led to a drastic decrease in the amount of money that these growth stage funds are putting out. I had lunch with a growth stage VC a couple days ago, he told me they're down 90 % in allocations this year versus last year. So that's, that's a huge amount of capital out of the system. And the other thing we're seeing is the types of companies that get funded. As interest rates rose, so the discount rate. And in consumer fintech, you had a lot of companies that were basically grow, grow, grow, grow at all expenses. Three year plus payback periods. Even some of the darling fintech companies were like two year payback periods. I think now we're seeing a return to the like, you got to be sub 12 month payback period. And I think that's, that's probably a good thing. We also saw in fintech in particular last year, everything, every consumer business getting funded, you had, we would always joke that someday a neobank for pets would get funded. And then I saw it, there was a neobank for pet owners that got funded. And it literally felt like every, every consumer business, you know, you slap a mobile app on it, and it would get funded. Unfortunately, as a lot of you guys know, customer acquisition just got really tough. Both increased competition, bass providers making it really easy to get a neobank set up. So things just got really competitive. And then you tack that on to the Apple and Facebook changes. And it became a really difficult customer acquisition, a time for customer acquisition. And as interest rates rose, we decided, hey, like, a lot of these companies are going to be really tough to fund going forward. And I think you're starting to see the domino effect of that interest rate rise today. And some of these companies aren't raising that next round of funding. So then you say, okay, well, what is getting funding? Surely, infrastructure is okay, right? Like we love fintech infrastructure. Well, unfortunately, these infrastructure players need to sell to someone. And if that someone is a consumer player, those companies are getting less funding. So there's less growth that's available to the infrastructure players as well. But I do think that there are opportunities in fintech, even though the repercussions go far and wide. And, you we've seen companies in our portfolio that had a tremendous revenue growth due to the interest rate hikes. We have companies that are storing a lot of capital on behalf of their customers. We had one company actually triple the revenue with the interest rate hikes. So there are some bright spots. And although the funding rate, the funding challenges started with late stage, they actually did come down to series A as well. As I mentioned, in 2021, our companies were raising crazy $100 million plus prices. This year, they've raised at much more modest prices, I'd say like 30 to 60, 70 has been what I've seen. So it's probably really just more of a return to sanity, something more akin to what we saw in 2019. Now, the one area where we've seen the least amount of change is seed funding. So somehow seed funding has stayed relatively consistent, maybe we're down 20%, but that's a far cry from every other stage down 50 % or more. I think there's a few reasons for it. One is, as I mentioned, there's a lot more capital in fintech, a lot of new funds, some new funds, I feel like are relatively priced and undisciplined. They have only seen an up market and are pricing things like an up market. But when you do the fund return map, it just does not work. And then we see later stage funds. So we were recently looking at a seed deal, and it was $3 million round. And it ended up getting done by a $12 billion fund. And you're like, why the hell is a $12 billion fund leading a $3 million round? And the answer is like, they're not doing any growth rounds, but they still want to be active. So they're investing at every stage. And they're a lot less price sensitive than other funds. So seed has held up, seed pricing has held up more than I would have expected. Now, the other thing is, even though valuations are down, round sizes are down, it still costs a lot of money to rent an apartment in San Francisco. And so it also costs a lot of money to hire an engineer. And that inflation has impacted everyone. So the price of hiring folks has stayed consistent. So you still need a certain amount of money to get your company off the ground. And that's what we're seeing. So what does the future look like? Well, I actually have no idea. I can tell you what today looks like. Today, I'd say like, in terms of pricing, we're seeing pre -seed rounds kind of return to the 2019 era. I'll say, and for us, we've done pre -seeds in the five to 10 range, seeds in the 10 to 20 or maybe a little bit higher for outstanding founders range. We're seeing series A's in the 30 to $70 million range. We're seeing series B's in the 100 to $150 million range. So, you know, things are down pretty significantly from where they were a year ago. I do think though, there will continue to be lots of capital available for great ideas and founders. But I do think, unfortunately, we're no longer the bell at the ball. Like people who changed their Twitter profile, the FinTech investor two years ago, then they changed it to Web3 investor. And today, they're just venture investor. So I think a little bit of the sheen has come off as we've seen, you know, the public markets fall in FinTech, we've seen it across the board. So I don't think we're going to get back to the multiples of 2021 anytime soon, which is very unfortunate for all of our portfolios. But I do think that there will be less competition out there. And there are lots of great folks in the market. So I think it's a great time, maybe as great a time as ever to buckle up and build a great sustainable business. And if you're doing that, I'd love to find you. So please talk to me. That's it.

Welcome, everyone, to the Informations TITV. My name is Akash Pasricha. It is Thursday, October 9th, and we are taking a full tour of the tech sector today, folks. We are talking about the booming business of batteries and power with a $1 billion funding round. We're also going to get into how AI is overhauling the business of sports and recapping a big event that we hosted on that topic at San Francisco Tech Week earlier this week. And finally, we've got our friends at Better Tomorrow Ventures coming on the show. We're going to talk about their newest funding round and about the future of fintech. Let's get started with the business of batteries, though. The AI boom and all of its power demands have brought a renewed focus on the energy sector at large, and that has meant several new power companies have been able to raise big funding rounds as of late. One of those companies is Base Power, a company that raised $1 billion this week at a valuation of roughly $3 billion. That figure is according to The New York Times. The company is just two years old, and to tell us more about their approach to all things electricity, I want to bring on the company's chief operating officer, Justin Lopez. Justin, welcome to the show. It's great to have you. Justin thanks so much for having me, and good to see you. Well, congrats on the funding round. There's a lot to get to. Look, I think before we get into understanding what the company does, we've seen the charts here. I think a lot of people know that electricity prices are going up, and they've been going up for quite a few months now. Help us understand what the root causes are there, and then we'll talk into how you guys are addressing that issue.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yeah, look, it's a fascinating time to be in the energy industry, particularly in the electricity industry. To answer your question, the electricity prices have been going up over the last several years, and this is due primarily to the cost of the delivery of the electricity. So folks might not know this, but there's really two components to the cost of energy delivered to your business or home. It's the cost of the energy itself and the cost to get it to you, which is really the cost of the grid. And if you look at the two components of that cost, the cost of getting it to you, the shipping costs, so to speak, have gone up quite meaningfully with the increase in demand from AI, as you mentioned,

[None]
electrification,

[SPEAKER_05]
EVs, et cetera, that's putting more load and more demand on the system. And frankly, not a lot of new technology and new business models to rebuild that system. And actually, the costs to generate the electricity in the first place has been coming down, somewhat counterintuitively, from advancements in solar and wind and natural gas, et cetera, over the last few decades.

[None]
Got

[SPEAKER_05]
it. So it's really, it's a demand issue right now, is the key point. Yeah, it's, I would say it's an infrastructure issue, even more so than a demand issue. All right, so we're going to talk about strategic pivots, something that's pretty close to my heart because a lot of my portfolio companies have been through them, and even myself, I've been through it myself as a founder. So I thought maybe we could start by talking through some companies that you guys all know, and I might tell you what the company started out as, and you have to tell me what the company is now. So first one's pretty easy. It's Bourbon, a very famous company today. It started out as a location sharing app, B -U -R -B -N. Does anybody know what that company is today? Correct. It's Instagram. So Instagram became a photo sharing app, but actually it was a location sharing app that they allowed folks to add photos to, and they realized the photo part was more popular than the location sharing part, and they pivoted the business to this filters app called Instagram. All right, another one. This one's kind of tough, actually. It's Chiquita, and this is a education app that allows teachers to share short -form video content on education. It's the app now known as TikTok. It actually started out as an education app, and so what happened was the founders built this product. They were educators. They started the product for teachers to teach their students various things in short form, and what happened was it accidentally caught on amongst people using it to do karaoke, and the founders realized that the app was getting a lot of popularity Thursday nights when there was this popular TV show called Carpool Karaoke, and they saw the videos, and it was all karaoke, and they pivoted the app to what was Musical.ly, which then got bought by Duyen in China and became TikTok. So another pivot. Okay, so another one. Odeo podcasting platform. came out a long time ago. Anyone know? Twitter, that's right. The founders all thought podcasting was the next new thing, and they launched a podcasting platform, but internally, they built this micro -blogging platform to talk amongst themselves. What happened with the podcasting platform was Apple released their own podcasting platform. Odeo was basically DOA, and they thought, okay, let's create this micro -blogging platform, Twitter. What is TinySpec? It was a gaming company started by Stuart Butterfield. Does anybody know now? Slack. They had built an internal tool. They built Slack internally for themselves, at the gaming company. Gaming company wasn't doing so hot. Some of their friends wanted the tool that they had built internally because they were all hyped about it. They started selling it externally, and then ultimately became, obviously, a massive company. And then the last one is one closer to my heart in the fintech space. It was a company called Wallet, and it was a consumer business that helped do you manage your finances. Anybody know this one? Wallet, the consumer company, didn't really take off that well and ultimately became Plaid. So they decided, we're going to sell the same product to other companies, building companies like Wallet. So anyway, just wanted to throw that out there that pivoting is not strange. Pivoting is not weird. You should not feel ashamed if your initial product doesn't work out. Many of the products that we use today were originally something else entirely. And so it's totally fine to pivot. And in fact, I think pivoting is really a sign of strength. So the way to think about it is, along the way, you're building a product, you have some idea of what it is you want to build, some idea of the future vision that you want to see in the world. And then along the way, maybe you realize customers aren't aligning with that vision. At some point, so then there's a question, how do you decide and when do you know that customers aren't aligning with that vision? Are you guys familiar with Rahul Vora, the CEO of Superhuman? He wrote this article in the first round review about how to find product market fit. How many of you guys read that article? Okay, we have a couple of people in back. So I highly recommend reading that article. It's a great tool for finding product market fit. And the question is simple. It's ask your customers how they would feel if they could no longer use the product. And if the response is not like overwhelmingly negative, and if it's not, oh, if this product didn't exist, my life would become a lot tougher, then you know you don't yet have product market fit. And a lot of times people think that they have product market fit because they're giving something away for free. So that's another thing I might challenge you with is thinking about pricing. In my portfolio, I have a company called Albert. It started out as a personal finance manager, actually like Wallet, the original product that Plaid was. So this company, you know, they were giving away a free product, help you manage your finances. And they actually didn't really have much monetization figured out. All the metrics look great. Like everybody was used. They had a lot of people signing up to try the product. But they realized, like, is this really critical? Like, do people really, really want this product? And the way that they decided to test that was actually charging their customers. And this is actually they did this when they were almost running out of money. So they were at the point where they were going to shut the company down. And they instead said, asked when customers logged into the app, they said, would you be willing to pay us for this service? And they had a slider. And the customers actually had to pay for the service. So you could pay zero, or you could pay up to $14 a month. And, you know, the company was dying at this point. So it was like a last ditch effort. Let's see if our companies are willing to if our customers are willing to pay.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_01]
the customers actually overwhelmingly were willing to pay, like 80 % of their customers were willing to pay an average of $4. And so they realized, okay, customers actually do want this product. And oh, by the way, that revenue actually saved them. And that meant that they didn't have to die. And actually, we're very quickly able to raise around that save the company. And today, the company is a massive company unicorn, etc. So I think one way to test if customers love your product is to charge them. So there's a couple other things that I think about a lot in pivots. One is, I recommend like trying to figure out as soon as possible. Usually, when you raise a seed round, you have 18 months, maybe 24 months of runway. And if you figure it out too late, if you're at the end of your runway, you know, it's going to be very difficult for you to survive and raise money. So what I like to say is, you know, within the first six months or so after launching your product, you should know if there's a strong customer pull. And if you're feeling that customer pull, it's going to be palpable. People are going to be talking about it with their friends. And you're going to get a bunch of customers that way. Like you're going to see tweets about it. investors are going to have heard about your company through their portfolio companies. So all that stuff is going to be happening. And if you're not feeling that immediately, you might need to pivot. And pivoting doesn't necessarily mean you change the business entirely from one thing to another. There are a lot of different ways to pivot. In the case of Albert, there was a small business model tweak, which was we move from a free service to a paid service. That's one type of pivot. Other companies in a similar space, like we mentioned Plaid, Plaid had built a similar product and pivoted to providing infrastructure that they had already built. So a lot of pivots are actually not wholesale changes like some of the ones we talked about earlier, but more smaller changes where you use the same product and sell to a different customer set. In fintech, it's very common for folks to start building a consumer product and realize that actually it might be better if you sell that product to banks. And banks can use that as a channel for their own customer acquisition. We see that quite frequently. So the other thing I want to talk about is, again, like this pivoting early concept. What I mentioned is like ideally in six months, you kind of know if the company, if you're, if you're feeling this market pull, if you don't feel it, it could also be that your product isn't quite there yet. Like you might have launched prematurely and that definitely happens. But what I'd encourage you to do to figure that out is talk to your customers. There's never a bad time spent talking with customers. What you should be focused on if you feel like you don't have product market fit. And even when you do is just talk to customers as much as you can and understand if they don't like your product, what is it that they don't like about your product? And if they do like your product, what would they like to see you change? And I will say it's easy to get into a paralysis from this because you might talk to 10 different customers and it's like the, like that terrible with the elephant. And like every customer tells you something different. But I do think overall, talking to customers and actually spending real time with them, having them go through your product helps you eliminate a lot of these problems and might help you understand a pivot. And sometimes a customer might say, well, I like this, but what I really need is something different. And we have a company in our portfolio that had a huge pivot. They were selling a product to hospitals and they realized after spending a bunch of time implementing with these hospitals, that the CIOs of these hospitals were actually telling them, this is great, but you know what would be even better. And they pivoted that product and now have had a lot of success and actually also went from a ACV in the tens of thousands of dollars to now an ACV annual contract value, in some cases, the millions of dollars with a single customer, truly incredible pivot. So the other thing to think about is when you do make a pivot, if it's a sharp pivot, you want to make sure that your team is on board. Like I've seen this happen. One thing we talked about was the idea of a fintech company pivoting from serving consumers to serving banks. Well, there's a big difference. And the team that helped you serve consumers may not be and probably isn't the same team that's going to help you sell into banks. Like you might have a bunch of great growth marketers that were helping you sell a product to consumers. Well, unfortunately, if you make that pivot, that team is probably less likely to be useful in your new company. As you do the pivot, I would, you know, try to first get alignment from the management team and make sure that that's what you want to do. It's actually okay to start in a small way. So you can originally do a bunch of tests. So maybe you have that consumer app going, but you test selling into banks. And if you're feeling a stronger market pull from the banks, then go in that direction and also pivot the team that way. If you do a wholesale pivot, like it's important to get buy -in from the entire team. It can be a real morale killer for somebody to feel like they weren't heard in the process. One thing I'll say on that is besides getting the team bot in, you also need to pivot how you think about the company. And so your metrics need to change. I always encourage people to have a few Nordstar metrics that they're always tracking and always talking about. So like in the case of Mercury, it might be deposits and customers. So there are a bunch of KPIs you need to track as a company. And as you execute the pivot, those KPIs also need to change. So as a team, what I would do is talk to them about the pivot. And as a team, define new benchmarks that align with the pivot. So you can measure that success of the pivot accurately. And this could still be the case while you're running the old business. If the pivot is a micro pivot while testing, you want to define what success looks like. The recap things I would say, pivot early because you have a limited runway. Within six months from launch, ideally, you have a sense on whether things are working. Use customer feedback as your Northstar. Continually talk to customers and get deep engagement with them. Don't just ask them questions. Try to actually sit next to them and talk to them, buy them a coffee. Make sure your team is aligned in the new direction. And remember, a lot of amazing companies pivoted. Pivoting can be the smartest thing you do as a company. And the final thing I'll talk about is because I'm an investor, you might wonder, well, what will our investors think? And what I'll say is investors want you to succeed. That's the most important thing. I do think it's important to talk to investors along the way. They can be a great sounding board. They might have seen other types of pivots and other types of companies doing what you're trying to do. So again, I would involve customers,

[None]
investors,

documents.text:
[SPEAKER_01]
Our first session in the America Zone today is a panel discussing the digital and cultural transformation in a post -COVID world. The panel is moderated by Conan French, IFF. Joining him, Dr. Lita Glyptis, Chief Client Officer at 10x Future Technologies, Matthias Kroener, founder and former chief executive of Fedor Bank, Nigel Verndon, co -founder and chief executive officer of Rails Bank, and Shil Mohat, founder at Better Tomorrow Ventures. Let's now join Conan and the panel for their discussion.

[SPEAKER_05]
Thanks very much, Glenn. And the title of the session was actually co -COVID world. And I think that that's a phrase that MD Ravi Menon and others have used to note that this isn't sort of a pandemic that we're just waiting for the post -COVID world, but that there are altered conditions that we'll be living with and working in for some time as society and financial services grapples with this new environment. So I always strive to have sessions be lively and informative. And with this group, I have no doubt that we will have a great and exciting session. So the first thing that I wanted us to really jump into is, how are financial service firms doing in the reaction to COVID? How are they doing in supporting society and its needs right now? And if you thought of this pandemic and the reactions to it as a referendum on digital transformation of the industry, what do the results look like? So Lida, maybe if we could start with you with your thoughts.

[SPEAKER_03]
It's an interesting question and one that we get asked a lot. And I must admit that I always frown a little bit when I hear representatives of financial institutions celebrating the amazing results they have had in terms of their coping and the policies they put in place. And not because they haven't, but because it's a mixed bag. So I would say that the majority of financial institutions have been ranging from pretty good to very good at coping with the immediate challenges of equipping their colleagues and their teams to deal with the immediate tasks at hand, throwing people at the challenge of creating payment holidays and sort of practical solutions, and providing bridges built with extraordinary human effort to actually deploy some immediate solace and immediate comfort. Have they been good at taking stock and making some radical bold moves down their digitization agenda? A digitization agenda that has been simmering for the last 15 years? I would certainly, I would say largely not. We have seen some extraordinary results that were the outcome of human effort, but we have also seen the limitations of the cautious digitization effort of the last few years. We have seen the gaps that not having truly digitally native capabilities give us. And we have also seen our reluctance, understandable, but also dangerous, to commit to the radical next move that would give us the infrastructure that would have made coping with the challenges a little bit easier. So how have they coped? Largely okay. Have they been able to really go out of their way to give something of a springboard to their communities? I would have say not, but they were not equipped for that.

[SPEAKER_05]
So Nigel, that same question to you, you know, making sure that things functions, making sure the sort of lights fit on, that people could work from home was sort of a herculine effort. But if we really think about a transformed world and living in conditions like this for a while, or, you know, a very different economy economy and landscape coming out of this, what are your thoughts on how the industry is done?

[SPEAKER_00]
Nigel I think, yes, everybody's put a great effort into to be able to work from home and other efforts. But I think there's a real reality slap of the billions that have been spent in the financial services industry in industry on digital transformation has really ended up in what colleagues and others call as a digital death zone. Because it's a place where analog processes have just been automated, as opposed to a true digital type of business. Now, this is an example of this. We clear sterling with the Bank of England directly, and also clear euros, we're all principal members of Visa, Moscow. We sent all our company home, and the customers didn't realise that we sent it out more than others, because we're used to dealing in a risk environment, having built companies through the dot -com bust and the credit crunch. But when the large institutions sending people home, there was definite impact to service. And that shows that there's still a lot of analog process, even in the digital channel, the apps, etc. So I think it's been a massive, massive wake -up call to actually realise that digital is not about having a digital channel. It's a mindset of removing friction from your processes, automation, etc. And if you look at Amazon, Amazon is essentially a logistics business. Google is a hardware, computer hardware business, if you look at it under the covers. And those still have the mindset of creating great digital product as frictionless to use for consumers, massively scalable, and have that ability. And just another observation is most financial institutions, only 3 % of them have any, on the boards, of people who've got a true digital background. And that's quite telling when you have to, I think, create the post of a Chief Digital Officer, because digital should be in your DNA. And I think we discussed last time the concept of we should have Chief Legacy Officer to make sure we don't do stupid things again. But this general concept that it's a DNA -led thing, and I think this, and I hope this is good for everybody, the boards and senior management of financial services firms, I think now realize, digital is a DNA thing. It's not something you create a post to do, because Google doesn't have a Chief Digital Officer, neither does Amazon, neither do we, neither do Fidel Bank, and others. I bet 10x doesn't either. So, this is the real difference. And I appeal to colleagues in the industry, let's all work together, because banks still need it, because they're sensors of safety, and run by very, very good people. People like ourselves around the table here are digital natives. I think if we actually work together, we kind of get better outcome for the person we care about, which is the consumer at the end of the day, and SMEs, and customers.

[SPEAKER_05]
Mattias, we'll dive into some of those questions that Nigel just brought up a bit later about culture, and how to drive transformation in the institution. But before we do that, I would imagine you have some thoughts on what COVID has shown on the digital transformation of the industry, and what you think the landscape looks like, how they've done so far.

[SPEAKER_04]
Conan, that is so sad, because I really wanted to follow up to Nigel with his points, and we had so much fun talking about the chief incumbent officer.

[None]
I really

[SPEAKER_04]
call for that position, and I'm sure out of some banks, we will have some applications for that. No, but joking aside, actually, I do not see any progress of incumbents becoming digital, right? As Nigel said it, and Lita said it, it's a holistic topic. It's definitely not only technology, and participating in a Zoom call doesn't make you a digital native, right? So it's about corporate culture, it's in particular about the target operating model, it's about your data management, it's about innovative technologies that we could apply in financial services from Bitcoin to smart, sorry, from blockchain to smart contracting, and so on and so forth. I would not see anything so far. I think yes, what we have to say, the incumbents definitely, and the players in the market definitely did do a very good job on their resilience in terms of emergency plans, moving out of the offices, going to home office, and so on and so forth. But in banking, that shouldn't be an issue, should it? Because in banking, we have no goods to carry with us, and maybe packages to sell to our customers. It's the money, it's wired anyhow, you know, 80 -98 % of the goods we are dealing with are technical anyhow. So what is the deal about it? We just made it, okay? And what we've realized is that what decades of consultancy actually couldn't deliver, a simple virus did. Suddenly, everybody's aware of that, everybody's talking about it, and so on and so forth. At the end of the day, we are not at the end of the day today. I think it's too early to call. And we have, yes, we see operational resilience, great. We see digital not achieved. We see some points of the backlog maybe working on, but the backlog list is still very, very long. And then we come back to banking itself. We definitely will see stress on the balance sheets. And there we could see again, did they use technology maybe for collection process and so on and so forth or not? Or do we stick with the traditional way of handling it? I think it's too early to call and we will see some maybe negative surprises.

[SPEAKER_05]
So, Shail, we're starting to see some of those results and surprises. Industry has been stressed by this cycle. The fintech sector has been stressed or in some cases accelerated by the cycle. But what's your view on how institutions have done so far?

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah. mean, I think from a fintech perspective, it's been phenomenal. It's like our portfolio companies are growing faster than ever before. The transformation from e -commerce has grown nearly 50 % year over year. So the payments associated have grown quite a bit. Branchless banking has accelerated in the US very substantially. The neobanks have done exceptionally well. You know, it's funny because I come from a more traditional background. worked in consulting, primarily serving financial institutions. At that point, we were still growing branch footprint. And now, of course, it matters less and less. And then in our insurance portfolio, it's been really phenomenal. All these startups have really been significantly benefited by COVID, you know, fortunately and unfortunately. In insurance, for example, you know, like our life insurance company, for our startup life insurance company, you don't need to go to a doctor to get a test. Like it's all done online via an app versus a traditional life insurance company, you do need to get to meet with a doctor. It's been a huge boon for us. So all in all, this has been a time that fintechs have really come in and offered a service that consumers needed during this time.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yeah. And you brought up a good point, which is that this crisis has really accelerated and amplified a lot of consumer adoption. That's something that sometimes takes years or decades to drive. And we saw it in a matter of days around the world simultaneously, which was one of the really remarkable things about this. And, you know, as we heard in the earlier session, there's been some, I think, relief in the legacy banking and financial services world and regulators and supervisors that kind of the functionality worked, the bare minimum was met, society could keep going on. And there was, I think, a huge sigh of relief. But if we really want to raise our aspirations from just supporting those minimal functions and just digitizing the legacy, you know, banks and insurers and institutions, know, what do we, Nigel, wanted to come to you and see what do we really need to thrive while serving the future needs of society and some of the things that have been revealed by this crisis?

[SPEAKER_00]
Sure. It's my soapbox subject. So, I'm ready for two hours of talking out. But one of the reasons we set up at Rails Bank is we have a firm belief that access to financial services is a human right right and not a privilege. But I'm pretty sure anybody in the financial services world pretty much thinks the same. And if you look at the people's core values. One of the key issues, though, is the cost structure of the industry, especially banking, just prevents that. Because if you've got somebody who's built absolute minimum, on living on a few dollars or so, or so, and it costs you 15 to 25 bucks a month to operate a current account, how can you bank them? It should be down at 10 cents. So, the space which my co -founder Clive and I were looking at is how do we change your cost structure? We looked at parallels in other industries. And that lovely word of deconstruct everything down to its core components, which in any way has worked in consulting probably makes a good few quid selling that type of thing. But what it fundamentally means is if you look at Apple, Apple took the music industry and deconstructed it down to a simple thing called a track and a digitized track. It's for 99 cents. And that meant that A, it was available everywhere. B, it was affordable. C, it could be reconstructed and put into new forms and then to mix it into a format that you want as a consumer and it could be wrapped around the consumer. And so you had a perfect storm because you took away the LP and the form factors and you created something that didn't have something physical. If you do that to financial services, which is essentially what we've been doing for the past four years, is the same thing. You can offer product and deconstruct it and then reconstruct some bank account from us or another provider, payments from another, cards from another, and construct product around the consumer that works for the consumer that moment in time. And so it helps, that can help, I think, move the industry forward massively. And we did an announcement today, which I won't plug at the moment, but to look at our Houston product. It is also taking inspiration from, again, what Apple did originally. They made the personal computer point and click because they deconstructed how you interact with it. They deconstructed the music industry into the track. And I think if we deconstruct and work on deconstructing the financial services industry into its absolutely core components and rebuilding them around the consumer, which is this whole embedded finance movement, we've got something that does change the world. And it does mean that people who need access to finance to get it. What it does do is put up an awful lot of challenges because it changes it from being financial services, financial company or institution centric to suddenly being customer centric, customer choice. Amazon's done this, so has eBay in their respective industries. And so that's what I think is the real challenge is, can we transform the legacy into work in a deconstructed world? Because all the products fundamentally they're offering, a current account or checking account, a payment and stuff are all exactly the same. There's nothing differentiated about them and things. So that's where we see, that's why CU is where I think the challenge, that's what we've been working on and delivering.

[SPEAKER_05]
And it sounds deceptively simple to put the customer at the center and really take a customer centric view on what the needs are when you think about products and services. But again, that can be really transformative across the institution. Shield, same question to you, what do firms need to do to thrive moving forward?

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah. I think it's really just being aware of what's coming and sort of, I'd say like, fortunately for us, our software companies tend to be younger and more nimble and able to thrive in different climates. So I think it's just keep doing what you're doing and they've done well.

[None]
Matthew,

[SPEAKER_02]
to you,

[SPEAKER_05]
what are some of those things that legacy institutions maybe should be learning from the firms and the practices that Nigel and Shield just sort of walked through?

[None]
Yeah. You know, if

[SPEAKER_05]
we aspire from just digitizing today or yesterday's bank, you know, what do they need to do?

[SPEAKER_04]
Well, you know, that buzzword really for years now is used to kind of heal everything. But I would say the problem is even deeper. You know, 35 years when I, 35 years back, I started my business career in hospitality. And actually I wanted to work at a bank those days only for one reason, because one of my professors at university, teaching me hotel administration and management that say, you need to work at the bank because the bank is the enemy. And I wanted to understand the enemy. And I wanted to know how the enemy is working, how the enemy is making a loan decision for me as a future hopeful hospitality manager. And actually I got stuck. Why? Because the bank managers those days actually came back to me and said, listen, in our organization, you are the only one with a customer centric banking thinking. Sorry. And customer centric banking was the outcome of that. But, you know, that that taught me that, OK, I came from hospitality and I'm the only one who is customer centric. So this is lesson number one. You obviously do not learn that in banking. Second, what I learned is that banks are used to take the regulator as an excuse for not being customer centric, you know, because then the bank and in the meantime, I have to say to the defense of the banking and financial services industry. Yes, sometimes this is exactly the case, you know, as a bank, you might even want to go and do something good and maybe take even more risk on your books because you think now in particular days we are living in society might need it. But believe me, next next minute, the regulator will ring your doorbell and say, listen, what are you doing there? And I think so. We have to have a look to the whole environment and and that includes the regulator as a stakeholder. And then thinking back when we founded FIDER now 10 years, more than 10 years ago, we had a what I called a strategic square on what we are operating because we as a bank, as a first step. And I think this is an exercise everybody must do did have a look to society, did identify a number of mega trends within this society and created that square out of it, which, you know, cornerstones to that was like everything will be mobile. People will do e -commerce. People will still use and massively use video games. You know, this kind of behavioral people will interact on social media platforms. And that was our cornerstone and we positioned our feeder bank concept. Well, hopefully in the middle and say, OK, these are the mega trends of society we want to work in. What kind of behavior on our customer side is to is to be expected so that we are a good partner for that? And this kind of exercise I do lack and do not see at all, because I would say the problem starts with banks not having an idea about a digital lifestyle is.

[SPEAKER_05]
Well, Lida, Matthias has mentioned some constraints that a lot of legacy institutions work under and you were responsible for innovation to large legacy institutions. And as you think about sort of that future that we've fast forwarded into this year of e -commerce, embedded finance, very distributed activities, what are some of the things that you think institutions need to do to really thrive and meet customer and society needs going forward?

[SPEAKER_03]
So I agree with everything that has been said, and I love the way in which it was said. And I feel slightly conflicted that I am always in defense of bankers. But I think there is something there is something worth flagging here. And it was said before, but let's tease it out. The the world that most legacy banks operate in is is a hybrid now because they have evolved from a time when a lot of what is now possible wasn't. And their technologies are in their state. It comes with immense complexity. Some systems still carry behaviors from a time when real time connectivity was not possible, let alone desirable. And therefore, the transition of digitizing and trying to keep the shop running while transforming comes with a lot of challenges that have been described. Have the banks been learning? Yes. Yes. Are the banks coming to the table to to talk to Fedor back in the day about white labeling their platform, to talk to Rails Bank, to talk to us at 10x about what the future needs to look like? And are they going on a journey that is hard? Yes. But is it fast enough? And I would say that the biggest realization that has come to banks in the last few years is twofold. One is the bank is no longer in control of the timing. For those of us who have been on the banking side for a very long time, we know that we felt that we had choices to make and we had the time in which to make them in a way that felt comfortable. And banks have realized, be it the virus, be it the rapid digitization of life around us, that they no longer control the timing. The second piece, Matthias already mentioned, but it's worth stressing, the regulator used to be the thing that a lot of banks hid behind. Now the regulator has a profound understanding of what is possible and the value it brings for customers and consumers. So they create accelerated pathways that say to banks, we will give you time to do what you need to, but we will no longer give you air cover. And those big realizations, it's not our tell, the timing is not in our control and the regulator expects better because they know better is possible. It's creating an accelerant for the banks. And it's not easy, but I do believe that we're getting to the point where it's inevitable.

This is Siddharth Alwalia. Welcome to the 100x Entrepreneur Podcast. This episode is brought to you by Prime Venture Partners and Early Stage VC Fund led by Amit Somani, Sripati Acharya and Sanjay Swami. Prime is often the first institutional investor in category creating tech startups in fintech, SaaS, healthcare and education such as MyGate, quizzes, mfine. To know more about Prime visit primevp.in. Today I have with me Shil Monaut, founder of Better Tomorrow Ventures. Shil has been an entrepreneur two times and both his journeys, you know, he saw a successful exit via acquisition. With Better Tomorrow Ventures, Shil typically invests at seed and pre -seed stage riding between 500,000 to 1.5 million check. Welcome Shil to the 100x Entrepreneur Podcast. Thank you for having me Siddharth. Shil, we'd love to know about your journey as a founder and then as a VC. Yeah, absolutely.

[SPEAKER_01]
So my journey as a founder, I guess even before I was a founder, starts my journey, let's talk about my journey in fintech, financial technology. It starts out on the nonprofit side. I actually spent some time working on the nonprofit side in with this nonprofit called Kiva. Kiva is a website that allows individuals from the developed world to make loans to individuals in the developing world for the sake of alleviating poverty. And I actually moved to India to work on this project. And, you know, through that, through the course of Kiva, we've done several billion dollars of loans, all at 0 % interest. But this, you know, although it's a nonprofit, we really operated like a startup. And we had a lot of really influential people guiding us. We had Reid Hoffman on our board. We had Keith Robois involved very early on. So this is my first foray into fintech and ended up being a foray into startups as well. And so I really enjoyed that. But before and after that, I was in consulting. I worked at BCG serving financial institutions. And then another buddy of mine from BCG had an idea for a company. Meta is a contender. I think there's no reason why Meta could not win in this space.

[SPEAKER_01]
All right, let me give you the one reason people don't trust them. And that is an unholy combination. My perspective is people already distrust this company. I was really looking forward to trying it. But I connected my Gmail, and it just felt left me so uneasy that I just connected it, you know, within hours. Not only that, when I had it connected, the conversational flow, its ability to do things, I found was worse than what I get with ChatGPT. So for Meta, you have a company that is trusted less and a company with worse AI. And it's telling everybody, trust us more, use our inferior product for some use cases that you can find elsewhere. I just found it unconvincing. To me, when it comes to Meta, I just think that they're in this long stage of denial, or they think that they're going to ship AI products that people will use, and they should just cut to the chase, become a NeoCloud, rent out those GPUs, rent the data center, and give up on this dream that's never going to materialize.

[SPEAKER_00]
Okay, so I have a lot of things to say here. One, I mean, you're absolutely right. Trust is Meta's biggest structural weakness in this category. And trust matters more here than it does in social media. And I think they have done a bad job on the PR front to date. But I think you'll see, you know, in that announcement, they really led with the trust factor. And they said, they're actually not going to use this data to better personalize your ads, which upsets me personally, like, I want you to have that data. For me, like, if you could serve me a better ad for something that I want to buy, that's great. I want Meta to have more information on me, I would gladly hand over that information to Meta. I understand that most people are not like that. And giving it your email, your calendar, your payment information, having it take actions for you is something that people may not go along with. I think they will, those problems will be overcome when they see how powerful it is. And I think the average person does not actually care that much. If you could choose a powerful product versus, versus one that you have a little less privacy over, I think you're going to choose a more powerful product, especially one with network effects. Five years ago, everyone in my friend group said, we're switching off WhatsApp, we're moving to Signal. That lasted for about five days. And then we were all back on WhatsApp. I think it's a big deal for a certain subset of users. And I think Meta is doing a good job addressing that. I don't think it matters for that many people. Your second point was that Meta is not good at AI. And I think you're just behind the times here. I think their latest models are quite good. And frankly, for what you need this thing for, you don't need a frontier model. So it doesn't really matter. You don't need the work that Astra is doing and you can't afford it for this kind of thing anyway.

[SPEAKER_01]
All right. I'm going to strongly disagree with you on this one. Look, I think my contention here is, is not that Meta isn't any good. Clearly it made some progress on the benchmarks, but they're just not as good as OpenAI. And OpenAI is building this. And people intentionally come to Meta for AI. So they're predisposed to use an OpenAI product for something like this. And I do think that it is significant. And yeah, all right. You know, I think people tend to brush away these privacy issues if the product is really good. But if your product trails, which I would say it is right now to the OpenAI products, you're just going to have a harder time getting over that privacy barrier. It is, there is a trust and there's a capability side to the equation. Meta has less trust than OpenAI, even though OpenAI isn't crushing it on the trust factor and they have less capabilities. And so even if Meta, you know, might make a more user -friendly experience right now, OpenAI is going to catch up with it. And they're going to reverse, do the reverse to Meta that Meta has been doing to all these companies like Snapchat in the past, which is when they see a good product experience, they've got the billion users. They can copy that over. I'm talking about OpenAI, copy that over into ChatGPT.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_01]
they'll be the ones to cut off the growth and win here. So I would say, well -argued, Sheil, but I'm still not giving Meta the upper hand on this one.

[SPEAKER_00]
I think that's totally fair. And I wouldn't necessarily argue that Meta is going to win this race. And it's obviously extremely early innings where you have very few people on these products at all. I do think Meta has some inherent benefits. Now, I will say, a year ago, I would 100 % have believed that Google would own this. And Google, they have all my email. They have all my photos. They have my web browsing. They have all this rich information and context is super important in this product. But actually, it turns out that I was probably wrong because Google has my Gmail, but any other company can just plug into my Gmail and get all that information. And the same is true of many other products that Google has. And Google seems to have fumbled the bag here.

Welcome to another episode of Tank Talks. I'm your host, Matt Cohen. And on this week's episode, we welcome co -founder and general partner of Better Tomorrow Ventures, Shiel Manat. Shiel and I have a great conversation discussing his journey in and around the tech and venture capital ecosystem and how he made his way over to the Valley after selling his company to Groupon and then working out 500 startups as a fintech investor. Shiel and I also dig into how he started Better Tomorrow Ventures with his co -founder, Jake Gibson, co -founder of NerdWallet. and why he decided to spin out from 500 startups to start his own venture fund and seed it with his own capital. Shiel and I also discuss the power law in venture capital and how he's thinking about exits and returning capital to investors from his $150 million seed fund. Lastly, Shiel and I discuss his amazing experience sleeping at Brian Chesky's house, the founder of Airbnb, and how the authenticity and transparency in what Brian shared with him helped him think about building and investing companies better. Now let's jump into the tank for this week's episode with Shiel Manat, co -founder and general partner of Better Tomorrow Ventures. But before we get started today, as our listeners probably know by now, the team at Ripple is always focused on helping our founders and portfolio companies find the best partners to work with within the tech and venture capital ecosystem. And that is why we are so excited to announce our partnership with the incredible team at Tories LLP. When it comes to legal support and advice, the team at Tories is the best in class. Tories is a story Canadian law firm with offices in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary, Halifax, New York City, and Tories has been around since its founding in 1941. They have always worked closely with players across the emerging startup ecosystem in all aspects of the creation, acquisition, and commercialization of businesses. They help founders determine when and how much to fundraise, how to achieve the right economic structure, how to think about board and control issues, and how to successfully navigate different stages of growth. They are also advisors to VC funds, strategic investors, private equity funds, and other institutional investors on fund formation and shareholder arrangements to buyouts and other exits. In fact, Tories recently acted as counsel to Mavericks Private Equity on the transformative $260 million MyoVision Technologies Growth Funding Round with an advisory team that included Danny Asif, Konata Lake, and Max Schwartz Label on that investment. So whether you are negotiating a new business arrangement or developing a new service offering, Tories helps clients seize new opportunities and build creative, market -leading business models in this fast -paced world we live in every day. So visit Tories.com to learn more. Thanks for joining us in the tank today, Shiel.

[SPEAKER_02]
Welcome to Breaking Banks.

[SPEAKER_05]
Hey, Breaking Banks. Are you looking forward to next year? I can tell you I am ready to be done with this one. As we approach the end of a very disruptive and chaotic year, let's talk about what 2021 might hold for financial services, fintech, and venture capital. On this episode, we're speaking to Debbie Bianucci, Chief President and Chief Executive Officer of BAI, to hear her thoughts on the last 11 months and predictions for the new year. And in the second segment, I'm joined by Shiel Minot and Jake Gibson of Better Tomorrow Ventures to discuss BTV's $75 million raise and how they're having a positive impact in helping the world of entrepreneurs really create a better tomorrow. Then, stay tuned for a quick update as Brett King hosts Charles Green, founder and CEO of RFI Group, to hear about a recent strategic growth investment RFI Group received from Diversus Capital Partners that will allow RFI to expand their footprint and data services. So, Debbie, for those who might not be as familiar with BAI, can you share a little bit about your mission and who your constituents are?

[SPEAKER_00]
Sure. We're, you know, we're a leading industry organization. We don't do any lobbying. Our purpose is to support financial services leaders as they run their business. And we work with banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, fintechs, all different kinds of financial services companies to help them make better decisions about their business business, with research, education, and various kinds of thought leadership.

[SPEAKER_05]
So, you know, it obviously has been a pretty interesting year. And I'm guessing a lot of these organizations have leaned heavily on you. What are your observations, you know, when historians write the history or do the study of 2020? What do you think it meant for financial services?

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, it certainly was a year of disruption. And, you know, Jason, it was one that was unlike anything I've seen in my career. And I mean that in a good way, because what happened with the banks is they were thrust into the situation like we all were. But they moved faster. They made bolder decisions. And they delivered for their colleagues and their customers in ways that no one ever thought was possible in the toughest of circumstances. And what I think that means for them is that they have learned what can happen to be more nimble and to move faster. And the disruption that they experienced, even though it was thrust upon them, is going to forever change the way that the industry works. I mean, I'll give you an example, because the PPP loans that were handled all by the banks, the banks did over 5 million loans in four months.

[None]
Yeah.

[SPEAKER_00]
When the SBA did about 70,000 in all of 2019. And so it demonstrates what the banks can do if they think differently about how to approach their business. And if you think about digital adoption, the way in which consumers have changed the way they want to interact with the banks, the banks had to figure that out quickly. And it worked. So I think the industry has forever changed, but in a much better way.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yeah. It really did change from the we can't to the we must.

[None]
And a lot of

[SPEAKER_05]
those naysayers, I think, within the organization, you know, couldn't use the political power of, you know, but this is the way we've always done it. Or, oh, those tech companies can do that, but we could never do that. The incumbents really did, you know, break down a lot of that scar tissue.

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, it's a little bit of, you know, be careful what you pray for, because the banks have for a long time planned and wanted to have their customers change the way they interacted. Not so dependent upon the branch using the digital channels. And then suddenly it happened. And I think the way you described it is accurate in a way that the banks were much more action oriented and willing to take some more risks, in part because they were motivated to keep their customers and colleagues safe, but make sure that they could get their banking done.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yes. Were there any changes that you expected that you didn't see more of?

[SPEAKER_00]
That's a great question, because I think the the changes that occurred as the banks were evolving from if you think about going back to early March to mid March, and then through each month as we went through the pandemic and the period of social unrest that began maybe in the April, May timeframe. The banks challenges were changing during those times. But probably what I thought we would see more of is sustained change in the way in which the branch delivery and contact center delivery were initially changed and that they would have gone on for longer. But it was really interesting to see how the challenges they faced changed almost week to week. So as soon as they thought and figured something out, then the next week it was a new challenge they had to figure out, which was part of what perpetuated this agile, bold, more flexible decision making that really made a difference in the pandemic. Right.

[SPEAKER_05]
The, you know, call it the series of waves that, you know, came at them, you know, like a set, not just a single wave. I think that's an important aspect to what really moved them, because you can't say, oh, I'm going to be the fast follower, I'm going to wait and see how this plays out and then I'll respond, you know, which is, let's face it for a lot of incumbent financial institutions, that's what they do. But that insight you just had around if you waited, you know, now you're just stacking up challenge upon challenge, you know, so you have to be in the moment with the decision making.

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, that's absolutely true. And one of the things that we found and one of the things that we do at BAI is to help facilitate the collaboration across the banks in the industry, which when COVID hit, there had to be fast connections made so that the banks could compare notes. And Jason, all the secret sauce went out the window because there's nothing in competitive advantage to try and figure out how to keep your employees safe, for example.

[SPEAKER_05]
Yep.

[SPEAKER_00]
And so we found that the collaboration and the ability to compare notes on the questions they were facing and the alternatives that they were considering really helped them because they could make better decisions in the context of knowing what the other banks were doing.

[None]
Do

[SPEAKER_05]
you think this is going to change decision making structures organizationally? Are you seeing changes made within the bank or the insurance company or the credit union?

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, know, it's really hard to generalize on that because there are so many different organizational structures. But if you had to pick one thing that probably is changed is the courage associated with doing things faster and trying things and managing them in a more real time basis. So you try something, it doesn't work, you evolve it, and that's what agile is all about. And so while I don't know that you could generalize about the way structures might change or decision processes might change, what is changing is it'll happen faster. And that's good for customers because the banks will be able to be more responsive, banks, insurance companies, mortgage companies, etc.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_05]

[SPEAKER_05]

[SPEAKER_00]

[SPEAKER_05]
Yeah.

[SPEAKER_00]

And what we can see, Jason, is that the customers who have adopted new channels and digital capabilities so quickly during the pandemic, are telling us that they want to continue with that. [SPEAKER_05]
And I think, you know, part of that we're seeing more and more encroachment by the large technology companies that are only extending that reach in digitization, you know, with Google entering the fray to be partnering with banks, with Stripe and, you know, beginning to work with Goldman Sachs, that it isn't just the digital drive internal to financial services. There's a digital drive, you know, coming from the side as well.

[SPEAKER_00]

[None]
other

[SPEAKER_00]
important topics, not to mention digital transfer information and product issues and so forth. I do think that the US continues to lag Europe on important areas of evolution, including open banking.

Who should I vote for? So some of these just simple things that seem simple, like a voting guide are actually very valuable. Um, and I think, you know, now grow SF itself is a force in local politics, which is, which is very exciting.

[None]
Um, and I

[SPEAKER_01]
Um, I, yeah, I, do think we've seen another example at a state level would be, um, insurance. So obviously there were, um, the fires in LA, uh, in January were incredibly destructive. And I think a lot of people for the first time realized the reason that they were so destructive in part, and the reason why people didn't have insurance is in part due to the poor state of insurance. And that's in part the regulatory state and in part our insurance commissioner, Ricardo Lara, who has no training in insurance. He has like a bachelor's in journalism or something, and then became our insurance commissioner does not understand much about insurance. Um, and the state insurers have been complaining for a long time. And we, of course, have other major problems with insurance, uh, including the state needing to approve regulatory filings and, uh, and sort of watchdog organizations getting paid, uh, to fight every new regulatory filing. Just makes for a really dysfunctional state. And I think, uh, people did not have any idea about that stuff. And probably, you know, today in May, it's been a few months and people have already forgotten, but, you know, they might keep, they might, they might remember some aspect of it and think about that when it, when the next election comes around.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. Yeah. last guest, um, who's in the controller's office in LA said, described it as we have an attention deficit democracy. Like people just, you know, you don't pay attention to issues until it's broken. But also I think that's how like the regulatory state and policy ought to work. It's kind of like your like it security system. Like you don't want to think about defeating every, uh, DDoS attack that's coming across like at our website. Like you

[None]
just want to know my

[SPEAKER_00]
website's secure and that it's working. I think with policy too, it's like, you don't want to think and wake up. Like most people are, is our insurance system working well in the state right now? we have a big wildfire, like you don't want to think about it. Um, but then when it doesn't work, you know, it then draws people's attention to it, but then hopefully can be motivated to create fixes. Cause I know with the grow SF founders, co -founders, were talking about how like the school board recalls and some of those moments during COVID, it really got the average San Franciscan who typically may not have thought about politics to think about it. And then as a result, they were able to use that energy and that momentum to generate change. Um, so I think like the, it takes those moments of outrage of people asking, like look, shining a light on a situation and saying what the heck's happening here to then, uh, you know, engage in a way that hopefully can change it for the better. Well, yeah, absolutely. One question I wanted to always end on is kind of like, what's your, what's your hope for the future of California? You know, let's say we're talking again in 10 years, like what are some of the changes and things that you hope we, I mean, we already answered this with housing and other things like that. Is there anything else that you just hope for, for the future of the state, um, that gets you excited about the future?

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah, I think it's just like, it's such an exciting and beautiful place to live. And I think it's always going to draw the brightest people in the world to it. And I, you know, I think certainly, you know, there are ways that, that California can mess things up, but I'd love to see a lot more bringing back to the earlier topic, less theater, more experimentation. Like we have this world -class talent. Um, you know, it's one of the, just California by itself would be, I think the fourth.

[None]
Fourth, was like two

[SPEAKER_01]
weeks ago. Yeah. By GDP in the world. Um, and so that's, that's amazing. Um, and, uh, I think we, we, and then we, we have like that plus this beautiful place with extremely talented and smart people. And, um, it just makes me so happy and proud to be, uh, a California to be honest.

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, I'm proud of your California too. Thank you for your time. She'll really appreciate you taking time today to talk to me.

Absolutely.

We'll
